Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an established treatment option for patients with severe aortic stenosis across a broad range of surgical risk profiles. As the number of patients undergoing TAVI continues to grow and long-term survival improves, structural valve deterioration and the need for repeat interventions are increasingly encountered in clinical practice.

In this setting, transcatheter aortic valve-in-transcatheter aortic valve (TAV-in-TAV) procedures have emerged as a viable strategy for managing failed transcatheter prostheses. However, such interventions are associated with specific anatomical and technical challenges, including the risk of coronary artery obstruction and a reduced effective orifice area resulting in severe prosthesis-patient mismatch. These challenges are further amplified in sequential reinterventions, such as transcatheter aortic valve-in-transcatheter aortic valve-in-transcatheter aortic valve (TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV), where multiple overlapping valve frames must be carefully considered.

Evidence regarding serial transcatheter valve reinterventions remains limited, particularly in patients with a history of prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE). In such complex scenarios, detailed preprocedural imaging, individualised risk assessment and multidisciplinary decision-making are essential to determine feasibility and optimise procedural outcomes.

This case illustrates the role of CT-guided planning and strategy-driven transcatheter intervention in a patient with multiple prior TAVI procedures and treated PVE, highlighting key considerations for lifetime management of structural valve disease.

section_text:
Patient, a man in his late 70s, was admitted to the Academician E.I. Chazov National Medical Research Center after he presented with dyspnoea, a spastic sensation in the left side of the chest during physical exertion (walking distances of 200–300 m), dizziness and fatigue.

His medical history was notable for arterial hypertension, three-vessel coronary artery disease and multiple percutaneous coronary interventions performed in 2009 (right coronary artery), 2010 (left anterior descending (LAD) artery), 2012 (recurrent LAD intervention) and 2014 (circumflex artery). Additional comorbidities included third-degree atrioventricular block requiring pacemaker implantation (2014), type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and recurrent episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding since 2022.

In 2014, due to progressive aortic valve degeneration and severe stenosis, the patient underwent transcatheter implantation of a 27 mm Lotus valve (Boston Scientific). By December 2021, symptoms of exertional dyspnoea had worsened, and echocardiographic findings were consistent with severe bioprosthetic valve stenosis. By early 2022, the mean gradient had increased to 83 mm Hg, and ejection fraction (EF) had declined further to 42% (from 54% in December).

In May 2022, the patient underwent a TAV-in-TAV with implantation of a 23 mm Evolut valve (Medtronic). The procedure was complicated by the development of a pulsatile femoral haematoma and pseudoaneurysm, requiring open vascular surgery.

Following the Evolut TAV-in-TAV, the patient’s left ventricular EF improved from 42% to 54%, indicating a favourable early haemodynamic response. He was managed with guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure, including beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors and diuretics as indicated.

3 months later, in September 2022, the patient was hospitalised again with persistent fever and worsening heart failure symptoms. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed severe restenosis of the aortic valve prosthesis (mean gradient 35 mm Hg). Blood cultures were positive for Enterococcus faecalis, and a diagnosis of PVE was made. The patient received a full course of targeted antimicrobial therapy for PVE caused by E. faecalis, including 6 weeks of intravenous ampicillin-based therapy, followed by oral treatment according to infectious disease specialist recommendations. At the time of the third TAVI procedure, antimicrobial treatment had been completed, and no long-term suppressive antibiotic therapy was ongoing. Clinical assessment, repeated blood cultures, transoesophageal echocardiography and multislice CT (MSCT) confirmed resolution of infection with no evidence of active endocarditis.

After completion of antimicrobial therapy and partial symptom resolution, follow-up in January 2024 revealed worsening prosthetic valve function, with severe aortic stenosis and moderate-to-severe regurgitation. The mean gradient was 49 mm Hg, and left ventricular EF had recovered to 66%.

A decision was made to proceed with reintervention. On admission in June 2024, TTE showed persistent grade 2–3 intraprosthetic aortic regurgitation, a mean transvalvular gradient of 49 mm Hg and a markedly reduced aortic valve area (AVA) of 0.5 cm², consistent with severe prosthetic valve dysfunction. The AVA was calculated using the continuity equation, based on left ventricular outflow tract measurements and Doppler-derived velocity-time integrals. Two overlapping bioprosthetic valves were visualised.

MSCT revealed a minimum lumen diameter of 13.7 mm in the Evolut prosthesis, confirming severe haemodynamic compromise and guiding procedural planning for a third transcatheter valve implantation (figure 1). Preprocedural MSCT was used to assess anatomical feasibility and the risk of coronary artery obstruction. The evaluation included analysis of coronary ostial height, sinus of Valsalva dimensions, valve-to-coronary distance and interaction between the frames of the previously implanted transcatheter valves. Particular attention was paid to the relationship between the anticipated neo-skirt and coronary ostia, as well as to the feasibility of high implantation to preserve coronary flow and future coronary access. These findings guided valve selection, implantation depth and procedural strategy, allowing the intervention to be performed without coronary protection.

Transoesophageal echocardiography was performed prior to the reintervention and confirmed the absence of active endocarditis or paravalvular complications.

A detailed chronological timeline of the patient’s clinical course is provided in online supplemental table 1 (case timeline).

Given the patient’s complex triple-stented anatomy, prior infective endocarditis and prohibitive surgical risk, the third TAVI was planned as a CT-guided, strategy-driven procedure with emphasis on coronary protection, commissural alignment and optimisation of the residual effective orifice area.

The procedure was performed under local anaesthesia using left radial and left femoral arterial access. Aortography with a pigtail catheter confirmed severe aortic regurgitation (figure 2).

A Safari guidewire was positioned in the left ventricle via the left femoral access. Balloon pre-dilation of the aortic valve was performed with a 22/40 mm catheter under rapid ventricular pacing (180 beats per minute). Simultaneous aortography confirmed that coronary flow remained unobstructed (figure 3).

A self-expanding bioprosthetic valve (Acurate neo2, size S) was implanted in the aortic position. The device was aligned with the Evolut valve leaflets—based on preprocedural CT modelling—to maximise the effective orifice area and reduce the risk of patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM).

Post-dilation was performed using a 20/40 mm balloon under rapid pacing to optimise valve expansion. Final aortography confirmed correct positioning, preserved coronary perfusion and the absence of both perivalvular and transvalvular regurgitation (figure 4).

Commissural alignment was taken into account during valve deployment to preserve coronary access and reduce future procedural complexity, guided by preprocedural CT imaging and fluoroscopic landmarks.

Procedural success and prosthetic valve performance were assessed according to the Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 criteria, including evaluation of haemodynamic function, presence of residual regurgitation and procedure-related complications.

TTE performed immediately after the procedure on 7 June 2024 confirmed successful deployment of the third transcatheter valve. The valve leaflets were mobile, with complete opening and no evidence of aortic regurgitation (grade 0). However, haemodynamic parameters indicated significant transvalvular gradients with mean gradient 67 mm Hg. The calculated AVA was 0.9 cm² (indexed AVA 0.4 cm²/m²), and the Doppler velocity index (DVI) was 0.24—consistent with severe PPM.

1 month after implantation, TTE showed marked improvement: mean gradient was 27 mm Hg, and AVA had increased to 1.1 cm². Left ventricular remodelling was observed, with a reduction in chamber volumes. There was no residual regurgitation, and valve function remained stable within the moderately stenotic range.

At 3.5 months, the patient remained asymptomatic with good exercise tolerance. No signs of heart failure or recurrent infection were noted. The prosthesis maintained good function, with sustained improvement in haemodynamic parameters.

At 1-year post implantation (June 2025), the patient remained clinically stable and active, without dyspnoea or signs of decompensation. TTE showed a mean gradient of 26 mm Hg, AVA 1.1 cm² and EF 65%. No valve-related complications, regurgitation or evidence of recurrent endocarditis were observed.

These findings confirm the durability of the result and suggest a sustained functional benefit of the TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV intervention in this high-risk patient.

This case highlights the decision-making process and technical challenges of performing a third TAVI in a patient with prior TAV-in-TAV procedures and a history of PVE.

While TAVI has become an established treatment for aortic stenosis, its use in patients with prior endocarditis remains controversial. According to the 2025 European society of cardiology (ESC) guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease and infective endocarditis, surgical valve replacement remains the recommended strategy in PVE, particularly in cases complicated by heart failure or uncontrolled infection. However, the guidelines emphasise that management should be individualised, taking into account infection control, surgical risk and anatomical feasibility.

The choice of TAVI as the initial treatment strategy in 2014 was driven by the patient’s high surgical risk and multiple comorbidities, making conventional surgical valve replacement unfavourable at that time. As the patient subsequently developed structural valve deterioration, a transcatheter redo strategy was pursued in 2022 to restore valve function while avoiding the risks of open surgery. Following successful treatment of PVE and in the absence of active infection, the decision to perform a third transcatheter intervention in 2024 was based on prohibitive surgical risk, complex anatomical considerations related to prior valve frames and CT-confirmed feasibility of a strategy aimed at preserving coronary flow and achieving acceptable haemodynamic performance.

The mechanism of prosthetic valve failure in this patient was likely multifactorial. While the episode of infective endocarditis may have contributed to leaflet injury and subsequent mechanical restriction, progressive structural degeneration of the transcatheter prostheses also played a significant role. Importantly, once infection was considered resolved and no long-term suppressive antibiotic therapy was required, the management strategy for prosthetic valve dysfunction aligned with that of patients without active or ongoing endocarditis. Therefore, procedural decision-making was guided primarily by anatomical feasibility, haemodynamic severity and surgical risk rather than by the prior history of infection alone.

In this case, the patient had completed antimicrobial therapy, showed no clinical or imaging signs of active infection and underwent thorough preprocedural evaluation, including TEE and MSCT, both confirming the absence of vegetations or paravalvular complications. Furthermore, the patient had a European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation (EuroSCORE II) of 27.36%, significant comorbidities (COPD, diabetes, prior gastrointestinal bleeding) and two previously implanted transcatheter prostheses with extensive stent integration into the aortic wall—all of which rendered open surgery particularly high-risk and technically hazardous. Given the deep fixation of prior valves, surgical intervention would likely have necessitated total aortic root and ascending aorta replacement.

Several case reports of TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV procedures have been published,37 highlighting various anatomical and procedural challenges. Our case adds to this limited body of evidence, with the unique context of post-endocarditis degeneration and preserved valve function at 1 year.

This case underscores the growing importance of lifetime management strategies in structural valve disease. With each transcatheter reintervention, considerations such as frame layering, commissural alignment, coronary reaccess and residual effective orifice area become increasingly complex. Long-term planning and early discussion of procedural trajectories are critical, even at the time of the first intervention—particularly in younger or high-risk patients.

The structural degeneration observed in this patient involved leaflet fibrosis from prior degeneration and probable mechanical restriction following infection. The clinical team proceeded with implantation of a third valve—a self-expanding Acurate neo2 prosthesis—based on preprocedural CT and 3D modelling that demonstrated feasibility and adequate coronary clearance (figures 1, 5 and 7). High implantation of the third transcatheter valve was a deliberate procedural strategy. Implanting the device at the level of the Evolut valve leaflets allowed fixation of the pre-existing leaflets against the stent frame, thereby preventing further reduction of the effective orifice area caused by inward leaflet folding. In addition, this approach minimised the formation of a neo-skirt below the coronary ostia and contributed to preservation of coronary flow and future coronary access. This strategy was guided by preprocedural CT assessment and was essential to achieving an acceptable haemodynamic result in a triple-stented anatomy. Despite the complexity of a triple transcatheter valve configuration, this approach proved technically feasible and reproducible when guided by detailed preprocedural imaging and a predefined implantation strategy.

The Acurate neo2 was selected for its supra-annular leaflet positioning, relatively low frame height and favourable haemodynamic performance in narrow anatomies. Its design supports commissural alignment, which was a key consideration in this case to preserve future coronary access.

A critical technical concern in TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV procedures is the risk of impaired coronary access due to multiple overlapping stent frames. Although commissural alignment was attempted, the cumulative mesh burden may still present challenges for future coronary interventions. This highlights the need for meticulous procedural planning in patients with known coronary disease or those in whom future access may be essential. Preprocedural CT enabled measurement of the landing zone, evaluation of frame interaction and estimation of valve-to-coronary distances, although full three-dimensional expansion analysis was not performed using dedicated software.

The disappearance of the transvalvular gradient after the third implantation can be attributed to a combination of optimised commissural alignment, effective post-dilatation and partial mechanical expansion of the prior Evolut frame, improving leaflet motion and central flow dynamics. While intentional frame fracture was not performed, high-pressure balloon post-dilation likely contributed to further radial expansion of the Evolut, enhancing valve function.

The procedure was performed under institutional approval for off-label use of the Acurate neo2 prosthesis. Shared decision-making involved the patient and his family, and the case was reviewed in a multidisciplinary heart team meeting, including interventional cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, imaging specialists and anaesthesiologists.

Should the current prosthesis fail prematurely, treatment options would be extremely limited. Surgical explantation would remain technically demanding and high-risk. Emerging catheter-based solutions such as bioprosthetic valve fracture or leaflet laceration (eg, bioprosthetic or native aortic scallop intentional laceration to prevent iatrogenic coronary artery obstruction (BASILICA) might be considered, although their feasibility and safety in triple-stented configurations remain uncertain.

This case highlights the decision-making process and technical challenges of performing a third TAVI in a patient with prior TAV-in-TAV procedures and a history of PVE.

While TAVI has become an established treatment for aortic stenosis, its use in patients with prior endocarditis remains controversial. According to the 2025 European society of cardiology (ESC) guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease and infective endocarditis, surgical valve replacement remains the recommended strategy in PVE, particularly in cases complicated by heart failure or uncontrolled infection. However, the guidelines emphasise that management should be individualised, taking into account infection control, surgical risk and anatomical feasibility.

The choice of TAVI as the initial treatment strategy in 2014 was driven by the patient’s high surgical risk and multiple comorbidities, making conventional surgical valve replacement unfavourable at that time. As the patient subsequently developed structural valve deterioration, a transcatheter redo strategy was pursued in 2022 to restore valve function while avoiding the risks of open surgery. Following successful treatment of PVE and in the absence of active infection, the decision to perform a third transcatheter intervention in 2024 was based on prohibitive surgical risk, complex anatomical considerations related to prior valve frames and CT-confirmed feasibility of a strategy aimed at preserving coronary flow and achieving acceptable haemodynamic performance.

The mechanism of prosthetic valve failure in this patient was likely multifactorial. While the episode of infective endocarditis may have contributed to leaflet injury and subsequent mechanical restriction, progressive structural degeneration of the transcatheter prostheses also played a significant role. Importantly, once infection was considered resolved and no long-term suppressive antibiotic therapy was required, the management strategy for prosthetic valve dysfunction aligned with that of patients without active or ongoing endocarditis. Therefore, procedural decision-making was guided primarily by anatomical feasibility, haemodynamic severity and surgical risk rather than by the prior history of infection alone.

In this case, the patient had completed antimicrobial therapy, showed no clinical or imaging signs of active infection and underwent thorough preprocedural evaluation, including TEE and MSCT, both confirming the absence of vegetations or paravalvular complications. Furthermore, the patient had a European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation (EuroSCORE II) of 27.36%, significant comorbidities (COPD, diabetes, prior gastrointestinal bleeding) and two previously implanted transcatheter prostheses with extensive stent integration into the aortic wall—all of which rendered open surgery particularly high-risk and technically hazardous. Given the deep fixation of prior valves, surgical intervention would likely have necessitated total aortic root and ascending aorta replacement.

Several case reports of TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV procedures have been published,37 highlighting various anatomical and procedural challenges. Our case adds to this limited body of evidence, with the unique context of post-endocarditis degeneration and preserved valve function at 1 year.

This case underscores the growing importance of lifetime management strategies in structural valve disease. With each transcatheter reintervention, considerations such as frame layering, commissural alignment, coronary reaccess and residual effective orifice area become increasingly complex. Long-term planning and early discussion of procedural trajectories are critical, even at the time of the first intervention—particularly in younger or high-risk patients.

The structural degeneration observed in this patient involved leaflet fibrosis from prior degeneration and probable mechanical restriction following infection. The clinical team proceeded with implantation of a third valve—a self-expanding Acurate neo2 prosthesis—based on preprocedural CT and 3D modelling that demonstrated feasibility and adequate coronary clearance (figures 1, 5 and 7). High implantation of the third transcatheter valve was a deliberate procedural strategy. Implanting the device at the level of the Evolut valve leaflets allowed fixation of the pre-existing leaflets against the stent frame, thereby preventing further reduction of the effective orifice area caused by inward leaflet folding. In addition, this approach minimised the formation of a neo-skirt below the coronary ostia and contributed to preservation of coronary flow and future coronary access. This strategy was guided by preprocedural CT assessment and was essential to achieving an acceptable haemodynamic result in a triple-stented anatomy. Despite the complexity of a triple transcatheter valve configuration, this approach proved technically feasible and reproducible when guided by detailed preprocedural imaging and a predefined implantation strategy.

The Acurate neo2 was selected for its supra-annular leaflet positioning, relatively low frame height and favourable haemodynamic performance in narrow anatomies. Its design supports commissural alignment, which was a key consideration in this case to preserve future coronary access.

A critical technical concern in TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV procedures is the risk of impaired coronary access due to multiple overlapping stent frames. Although commissural alignment was attempted, the cumulative mesh burden may still present challenges for future coronary interventions. This highlights the need for meticulous procedural planning in patients with known coronary disease or those in whom future access may be essential. Preprocedural CT enabled measurement of the landing zone, evaluation of frame interaction and estimation of valve-to-coronary distances, although full three-dimensional expansion analysis was not performed using dedicated software.

The disappearance of the transvalvular gradient after the third implantation can be attributed to a combination of optimised commissural alignment, effective post-dilatation and partial mechanical expansion of the prior Evolut frame, improving leaflet motion and central flow dynamics. While intentional frame fracture was not performed, high-pressure balloon post-dilation likely contributed to further radial expansion of the Evolut, enhancing valve function.

The procedure was performed under institutional approval for off-label use of the Acurate neo2 prosthesis. Shared decision-making involved the patient and his family, and the case was reviewed in a multidisciplinary heart team meeting, including interventional cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, imaging specialists and anaesthesiologists.

Should the current prosthesis fail prematurely, treatment options would be extremely limited. Surgical explantation would remain technically demanding and high-risk. Emerging catheter-based solutions such as bioprosthetic valve fracture or leaflet laceration (eg, bioprosthetic or native aortic scallop intentional laceration to prevent iatrogenic coronary artery obstruction (BASILICA) might be considered, although their feasibility and safety in triple-stented configurations remain uncertain.

section_text:
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an established treatment option for patients with severe aortic stenosis across a broad range of surgical risk profiles. As the number of patients undergoing TAVI continues to grow and long-term survival improves, structural valve deterioration and the need for repeat interventions are increasingly encountered in clinical practice.

In this setting, transcatheter aortic valve-in-transcatheter aortic valve (TAV-in-TAV) procedures have emerged as a viable strategy for managing failed transcatheter prostheses. However, such interventions are associated with specific anatomical and technical challenges, including the risk of coronary artery obstruction and a reduced effective orifice area resulting in severe prosthesis-patient mismatch. These challenges are further amplified in sequential reinterventions, such as transcatheter aortic valve-in-transcatheter aortic valve-in-transcatheter aortic valve (TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV), where multiple overlapping valve frames must be carefully considered.

Evidence regarding serial transcatheter valve reinterventions remains limited, particularly in patients with a history of prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE). In such complex scenarios, detailed preprocedural imaging, individualised risk assessment and multidisciplinary decision-making are essential to determine feasibility and optimise procedural outcomes.

This case illustrates the role of CT-guided planning and strategy-driven transcatheter intervention in a patient with multiple prior TAVI procedures and treated PVE, highlighting key considerations for lifetime management of structural valve disease.

Patient, a man in his late 70s, was admitted to the Academician E.I. Chazov National Medical Research Center after he presented with dyspnoea, a spastic sensation in the left side of the chest during physical exertion (walking distances of 200–300 m), dizziness and fatigue.

His medical history was notable for arterial hypertension, three-vessel coronary artery disease and multiple percutaneous coronary interventions performed in 2009 (right coronary artery), 2010 (left anterior descending (LAD) artery), 2012 (recurrent LAD intervention) and 2014 (circumflex artery). Additional comorbidities included third-degree atrioventricular block requiring pacemaker implantation (2014), type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and recurrent episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding since 2022.

In 2014, due to progressive aortic valve degeneration and severe stenosis, the patient underwent transcatheter implantation of a 27 mm Lotus valve (Boston Scientific). By December 2021, symptoms of exertional dyspnoea had worsened, and echocardiographic findings were consistent with severe bioprosthetic valve stenosis. By early 2022, the mean gradient had increased to 83 mm Hg, and ejection fraction (EF) had declined further to 42% (from 54% in December).

In May 2022, the patient underwent a TAV-in-TAV with implantation of a 23 mm Evolut valve (Medtronic). The procedure was complicated by the development of a pulsatile femoral haematoma and pseudoaneurysm, requiring open vascular surgery.

Following the Evolut TAV-in-TAV, the patient’s left ventricular EF improved from 42% to 54%, indicating a favourable early haemodynamic response. He was managed with guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure, including beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors and diuretics as indicated.

3 months later, in September 2022, the patient was hospitalised again with persistent fever and worsening heart failure symptoms. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed severe restenosis of the aortic valve prosthesis (mean gradient 35 mm Hg). Blood cultures were positive for Enterococcus faecalis, and a diagnosis of PVE was made. The patient received a full course of targeted antimicrobial therapy for PVE caused by E. faecalis, including 6 weeks of intravenous ampicillin-based therapy, followed by oral treatment according to infectious disease specialist recommendations. At the time of the third TAVI procedure, antimicrobial treatment had been completed, and no long-term suppressive antibiotic therapy was ongoing. Clinical assessment, repeated blood cultures, transoesophageal echocardiography and multislice CT (MSCT) confirmed resolution of infection with no evidence of active endocarditis.

After completion of antimicrobial therapy and partial symptom resolution, follow-up in January 2024 revealed worsening prosthetic valve function, with severe aortic stenosis and moderate-to-severe regurgitation. The mean gradient was 49 mm Hg, and left ventricular EF had recovered to 66%.

A decision was made to proceed with reintervention. On admission in June 2024, TTE showed persistent grade 2–3 intraprosthetic aortic regurgitation, a mean transvalvular gradient of 49 mm Hg and a markedly reduced aortic valve area (AVA) of 0.5 cm², consistent with severe prosthetic valve dysfunction. The AVA was calculated using the continuity equation, based on left ventricular outflow tract measurements and Doppler-derived velocity-time integrals. Two overlapping bioprosthetic valves were visualised.

MSCT revealed a minimum lumen diameter of 13.7 mm in the Evolut prosthesis, confirming severe haemodynamic compromise and guiding procedural planning for a third transcatheter valve implantation (figure 1). Preprocedural MSCT was used to assess anatomical feasibility and the risk of coronary artery obstruction. The evaluation included analysis of coronary ostial height, sinus of Valsalva dimensions, valve-to-coronary distance and interaction between the frames of the previously implanted transcatheter valves. Particular attention was paid to the relationship between the anticipated neo-skirt and coronary ostia, as well as to the feasibility of high implantation to preserve coronary flow and future coronary access. These findings guided valve selection, implantation depth and procedural strategy, allowing the intervention to be performed without coronary protection.

Transoesophageal echocardiography was performed prior to the reintervention and confirmed the absence of active endocarditis or paravalvular complications.

A detailed chronological timeline of the patient’s clinical course is provided in online supplemental table 1 (case timeline).

Patient, a man in his late 70s, was admitted to the Academician E.I. Chazov National Medical Research Center after he presented with dyspnoea, a spastic sensation in the left side of the chest during physical exertion (walking distances of 200–300 m), dizziness and fatigue.

His medical history was notable for arterial hypertension, three-vessel coronary artery disease and multiple percutaneous coronary interventions performed in 2009 (right coronary artery), 2010 (left anterior descending (LAD) artery), 2012 (recurrent LAD intervention) and 2014 (circumflex artery). Additional comorbidities included third-degree atrioventricular block requiring pacemaker implantation (2014), type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and recurrent episodes of gastrointestinal bleeding since 2022.

In 2014, due to progressive aortic valve degeneration and severe stenosis, the patient underwent transcatheter implantation of a 27 mm Lotus valve (Boston Scientific). By December 2021, symptoms of exertional dyspnoea had worsened, and echocardiographic findings were consistent with severe bioprosthetic valve stenosis. By early 2022, the mean gradient had increased to 83 mm Hg, and ejection fraction (EF) had declined further to 42% (from 54% in December).

In May 2022, the patient underwent a TAV-in-TAV with implantation of a 23 mm Evolut valve (Medtronic). The procedure was complicated by the development of a pulsatile femoral haematoma and pseudoaneurysm, requiring open vascular surgery.

Following the Evolut TAV-in-TAV, the patient’s left ventricular EF improved from 42% to 54%, indicating a favourable early haemodynamic response. He was managed with guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure, including beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors and diuretics as indicated.

3 months later, in September 2022, the patient was hospitalised again with persistent fever and worsening heart failure symptoms. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) showed severe restenosis of the aortic valve prosthesis (mean gradient 35 mm Hg). Blood cultures were positive for Enterococcus faecalis, and a diagnosis of PVE was made. The patient received a full course of targeted antimicrobial therapy for PVE caused by E. faecalis, including 6 weeks of intravenous ampicillin-based therapy, followed by oral treatment according to infectious disease specialist recommendations. At the time of the third TAVI procedure, antimicrobial treatment had been completed, and no long-term suppressive antibiotic therapy was ongoing. Clinical assessment, repeated blood cultures, transoesophageal echocardiography and multislice CT (MSCT) confirmed resolution of infection with no evidence of active endocarditis.

After completion of antimicrobial therapy and partial symptom resolution, follow-up in January 2024 revealed worsening prosthetic valve function, with severe aortic stenosis and moderate-to-severe regurgitation. The mean gradient was 49 mm Hg, and left ventricular EF had recovered to 66%.

A decision was made to proceed with reintervention. On admission in June 2024, TTE showed persistent grade 2–3 intraprosthetic aortic regurgitation, a mean transvalvular gradient of 49 mm Hg and a markedly reduced aortic valve area (AVA) of 0.5 cm², consistent with severe prosthetic valve dysfunction. The AVA was calculated using the continuity equation, based on left ventricular outflow tract measurements and Doppler-derived velocity-time integrals. Two overlapping bioprosthetic valves were visualised.

MSCT revealed a minimum lumen diameter of 13.7 mm in the Evolut prosthesis, confirming severe haemodynamic compromise and guiding procedural planning for a third transcatheter valve implantation (figure 1). Preprocedural MSCT was used to assess anatomical feasibility and the risk of coronary artery obstruction. The evaluation included analysis of coronary ostial height, sinus of Valsalva dimensions, valve-to-coronary distance and interaction between the frames of the previously implanted transcatheter valves. Particular attention was paid to the relationship between the anticipated neo-skirt and coronary ostia, as well as to the feasibility of high implantation to preserve coronary flow and future coronary access. These findings guided valve selection, implantation depth and procedural strategy, allowing the intervention to be performed without coronary protection.

Transoesophageal echocardiography was performed prior to the reintervention and confirmed the absence of active endocarditis or paravalvular complications.

A detailed chronological timeline of the patient’s clinical course is provided in online supplemental table 1 (case timeline).

Given the patient’s complex triple-stented anatomy, prior infective endocarditis and prohibitive surgical risk, the third TAVI was planned as a CT-guided, strategy-driven procedure with emphasis on coronary protection, commissural alignment and optimisation of the residual effective orifice area.

The procedure was performed under local anaesthesia using left radial and left femoral arterial access. Aortography with a pigtail catheter confirmed severe aortic regurgitation (figure 2).

A Safari guidewire was positioned in the left ventricle via the left femoral access. Balloon pre-dilation of the aortic valve was performed with a 22/40 mm catheter under rapid ventricular pacing (180 beats per minute). Simultaneous aortography confirmed that coronary flow remained unobstructed (figure 3).

A self-expanding bioprosthetic valve (Acurate neo2, size S) was implanted in the aortic position. The device was aligned with the Evolut valve leaflets—based on preprocedural CT modelling—to maximise the effective orifice area and reduce the risk of patient-prosthesis mismatch (PPM).

Post-dilation was performed using a 20/40 mm balloon under rapid pacing to optimise valve expansion. Final aortography confirmed correct positioning, preserved coronary perfusion and the absence of both perivalvular and transvalvular regurgitation (figure 4).

Commissural alignment was taken into account during valve deployment to preserve coronary access and reduce future procedural complexity, guided by preprocedural CT imaging and fluoroscopic landmarks.

Procedural success and prosthetic valve performance were assessed according to the Valve Academic Research Consortium-3 criteria, including evaluation of haemodynamic function, presence of residual regurgitation and procedure-related complications.

TTE performed immediately after the procedure on 7 June 2024 confirmed successful deployment of the third transcatheter valve. The valve leaflets were mobile, with complete opening and no evidence of aortic regurgitation (grade 0). However, haemodynamic parameters indicated significant transvalvular gradients with mean gradient 67 mm Hg. The calculated AVA was 0.9 cm² (indexed AVA 0.4 cm²/m²), and the Doppler velocity index (DVI) was 0.24—consistent with severe PPM.

1 month after implantation, TTE showed marked improvement: mean gradient was 27 mm Hg, and AVA had increased to 1.1 cm². Left ventricular remodelling was observed, with a reduction in chamber volumes. There was no residual regurgitation, and valve function remained stable within the moderately stenotic range.

At 3.5 months, the patient remained asymptomatic with good exercise tolerance. No signs of heart failure or recurrent infection were noted. The prosthesis maintained good function, with sustained improvement in haemodynamic parameters.

At 1-year post implantation (June 2025), the patient remained clinically stable and active, without dyspnoea or signs of decompensation. TTE showed a mean gradient of 26 mm Hg, AVA 1.1 cm² and EF 65%. No valve-related complications, regurgitation or evidence of recurrent endocarditis were observed.

These findings confirm the durability of the result and suggest a sustained functional benefit of the TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV intervention in this high-risk patient.

This case highlights the decision-making process and technical challenges of performing a third TAVI in a patient with prior TAV-in-TAV procedures and a history of PVE.

While TAVI has become an established treatment for aortic stenosis, its use in patients with prior endocarditis remains controversial. According to the 2025 European society of cardiology (ESC) guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease and infective endocarditis, surgical valve replacement remains the recommended strategy in PVE, particularly in cases complicated by heart failure or uncontrolled infection. However, the guidelines emphasise that management should be individualised, taking into account infection control, surgical risk and anatomical feasibility.

The choice of TAVI as the initial treatment strategy in 2014 was driven by the patient’s high surgical risk and multiple comorbidities, making conventional surgical valve replacement unfavourable at that time. As the patient subsequently developed structural valve deterioration, a transcatheter redo strategy was pursued in 2022 to restore valve function while avoiding the risks of open surgery. Following successful treatment of PVE and in the absence of active infection, the decision to perform a third transcatheter intervention in 2024 was based on prohibitive surgical risk, complex anatomical considerations related to prior valve frames and CT-confirmed feasibility of a strategy aimed at preserving coronary flow and achieving acceptable haemodynamic performance.

The mechanism of prosthetic valve failure in this patient was likely multifactorial. While the episode of infective endocarditis may have contributed to leaflet injury and subsequent mechanical restriction, progressive structural degeneration of the transcatheter prostheses also played a significant role. Importantly, once infection was considered resolved and no long-term suppressive antibiotic therapy was required, the management strategy for prosthetic valve dysfunction aligned with that of patients without active or ongoing endocarditis. Therefore, procedural decision-making was guided primarily by anatomical feasibility, haemodynamic severity and surgical risk rather than by the prior history of infection alone.

In this case, the patient had completed antimicrobial therapy, showed no clinical or imaging signs of active infection and underwent thorough preprocedural evaluation, including TEE and MSCT, both confirming the absence of vegetations or paravalvular complications. Furthermore, the patient had a European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation (EuroSCORE II) of 27.36%, significant comorbidities (COPD, diabetes, prior gastrointestinal bleeding) and two previously implanted transcatheter prostheses with extensive stent integration into the aortic wall—all of which rendered open surgery particularly high-risk and technically hazardous. Given the deep fixation of prior valves, surgical intervention would likely have necessitated total aortic root and ascending aorta replacement.

Several case reports of TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV procedures have been published,37 highlighting various anatomical and procedural challenges. Our case adds to this limited body of evidence, with the unique context of post-endocarditis degeneration and preserved valve function at 1 year.

This case underscores the growing importance of lifetime management strategies in structural valve disease. With each transcatheter reintervention, considerations such as frame layering, commissural alignment, coronary reaccess and residual effective orifice area become increasingly complex. Long-term planning and early discussion of procedural trajectories are critical, even at the time of the first intervention—particularly in younger or high-risk patients.

The structural degeneration observed in this patient involved leaflet fibrosis from prior degeneration and probable mechanical restriction following infection. The clinical team proceeded with implantation of a third valve—a self-expanding Acurate neo2 prosthesis—based on preprocedural CT and 3D modelling that demonstrated feasibility and adequate coronary clearance (figures 1, 5 and 7). High implantation of the third transcatheter valve was a deliberate procedural strategy. Implanting the device at the level of the Evolut valve leaflets allowed fixation of the pre-existing leaflets against the stent frame, thereby preventing further reduction of the effective orifice area caused by inward leaflet folding. In addition, this approach minimised the formation of a neo-skirt below the coronary ostia and contributed to preservation of coronary flow and future coronary access. This strategy was guided by preprocedural CT assessment and was essential to achieving an acceptable haemodynamic result in a triple-stented anatomy. Despite the complexity of a triple transcatheter valve configuration, this approach proved technically feasible and reproducible when guided by detailed preprocedural imaging and a predefined implantation strategy.

The Acurate neo2 was selected for its supra-annular leaflet positioning, relatively low frame height and favourable haemodynamic performance in narrow anatomies. Its design supports commissural alignment, which was a key consideration in this case to preserve future coronary access.

A critical technical concern in TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV procedures is the risk of impaired coronary access due to multiple overlapping stent frames. Although commissural alignment was attempted, the cumulative mesh burden may still present challenges for future coronary interventions. This highlights the need for meticulous procedural planning in patients with known coronary disease or those in whom future access may be essential. Preprocedural CT enabled measurement of the landing zone, evaluation of frame interaction and estimation of valve-to-coronary distances, although full three-dimensional expansion analysis was not performed using dedicated software.

The disappearance of the transvalvular gradient after the third implantation can be attributed to a combination of optimised commissural alignment, effective post-dilatation and partial mechanical expansion of the prior Evolut frame, improving leaflet motion and central flow dynamics. While intentional frame fracture was not performed, high-pressure balloon post-dilation likely contributed to further radial expansion of the Evolut, enhancing valve function.

The procedure was performed under institutional approval for off-label use of the Acurate neo2 prosthesis. Shared decision-making involved the patient and his family, and the case was reviewed in a multidisciplinary heart team meeting, including interventional cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, imaging specialists and anaesthesiologists.

Should the current prosthesis fail prematurely, treatment options would be extremely limited. Surgical explantation would remain technically demanding and high-risk. Emerging catheter-based solutions such as bioprosthetic valve fracture or leaflet laceration (eg, bioprosthetic or native aortic scallop intentional laceration to prevent iatrogenic coronary artery obstruction (BASILICA) might be considered, although their feasibility and safety in triple-stented configurations remain uncertain.

This case highlights the decision-making process and technical challenges of performing a third TAVI in a patient with prior TAV-in-TAV procedures and a history of PVE.

While TAVI has become an established treatment for aortic stenosis, its use in patients with prior endocarditis remains controversial. According to the 2025 European society of cardiology (ESC) guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease and infective endocarditis, surgical valve replacement remains the recommended strategy in PVE, particularly in cases complicated by heart failure or uncontrolled infection. However, the guidelines emphasise that management should be individualised, taking into account infection control, surgical risk and anatomical feasibility.

The choice of TAVI as the initial treatment strategy in 2014 was driven by the patient’s high surgical risk and multiple comorbidities, making conventional surgical valve replacement unfavourable at that time. As the patient subsequently developed structural valve deterioration, a transcatheter redo strategy was pursued in 2022 to restore valve function while avoiding the risks of open surgery. Following successful treatment of PVE and in the absence of active infection, the decision to perform a third transcatheter intervention in 2024 was based on prohibitive surgical risk, complex anatomical considerations related to prior valve frames and CT-confirmed feasibility of a strategy aimed at preserving coronary flow and achieving acceptable haemodynamic performance.

The mechanism of prosthetic valve failure in this patient was likely multifactorial. While the episode of infective endocarditis may have contributed to leaflet injury and subsequent mechanical restriction, progressive structural degeneration of the transcatheter prostheses also played a significant role. Importantly, once infection was considered resolved and no long-term suppressive antibiotic therapy was required, the management strategy for prosthetic valve dysfunction aligned with that of patients without active or ongoing endocarditis. Therefore, procedural decision-making was guided primarily by anatomical feasibility, haemodynamic severity and surgical risk rather than by the prior history of infection alone.

In this case, the patient had completed antimicrobial therapy, showed no clinical or imaging signs of active infection and underwent thorough preprocedural evaluation, including TEE and MSCT, both confirming the absence of vegetations or paravalvular complications. Furthermore, the patient had a European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation (EuroSCORE II) of 27.36%, significant comorbidities (COPD, diabetes, prior gastrointestinal bleeding) and two previously implanted transcatheter prostheses with extensive stent integration into the aortic wall—all of which rendered open surgery particularly high-risk and technically hazardous. Given the deep fixation of prior valves, surgical intervention would likely have necessitated total aortic root and ascending aorta replacement.

Several case reports of TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV procedures have been published,37 highlighting various anatomical and procedural challenges. Our case adds to this limited body of evidence, with the unique context of post-endocarditis degeneration and preserved valve function at 1 year.

This case underscores the growing importance of lifetime management strategies in structural valve disease. With each transcatheter reintervention, considerations such as frame layering, commissural alignment, coronary reaccess and residual effective orifice area become increasingly complex. Long-term planning and early discussion of procedural trajectories are critical, even at the time of the first intervention—particularly in younger or high-risk patients.

The structural degeneration observed in this patient involved leaflet fibrosis from prior degeneration and probable mechanical restriction following infection. The clinical team proceeded with implantation of a third valve—a self-expanding Acurate neo2 prosthesis—based on preprocedural CT and 3D modelling that demonstrated feasibility and adequate coronary clearance (figures 1, 5 and 7). High implantation of the third transcatheter valve was a deliberate procedural strategy. Implanting the device at the level of the Evolut valve leaflets allowed fixation of the pre-existing leaflets against the stent frame, thereby preventing further reduction of the effective orifice area caused by inward leaflet folding. In addition, this approach minimised the formation of a neo-skirt below the coronary ostia and contributed to preservation of coronary flow and future coronary access. This strategy was guided by preprocedural CT assessment and was essential to achieving an acceptable haemodynamic result in a triple-stented anatomy. Despite the complexity of a triple transcatheter valve configuration, this approach proved technically feasible and reproducible when guided by detailed preprocedural imaging and a predefined implantation strategy.

The Acurate neo2 was selected for its supra-annular leaflet positioning, relatively low frame height and favourable haemodynamic performance in narrow anatomies. Its design supports commissural alignment, which was a key consideration in this case to preserve future coronary access.

A critical technical concern in TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV procedures is the risk of impaired coronary access due to multiple overlapping stent frames. Although commissural alignment was attempted, the cumulative mesh burden may still present challenges for future coronary interventions. This highlights the need for meticulous procedural planning in patients with known coronary disease or those in whom future access may be essential. Preprocedural CT enabled measurement of the landing zone, evaluation of frame interaction and estimation of valve-to-coronary distances, although full three-dimensional expansion analysis was not performed using dedicated software.

The disappearance of the transvalvular gradient after the third implantation can be attributed to a combination of optimised commissural alignment, effective post-dilatation and partial mechanical expansion of the prior Evolut frame, improving leaflet motion and central flow dynamics. While intentional frame fracture was not performed, high-pressure balloon post-dilation likely contributed to further radial expansion of the Evolut, enhancing valve function.

The procedure was performed under institutional approval for off-label use of the Acurate neo2 prosthesis. Shared decision-making involved the patient and his family, and the case was reviewed in a multidisciplinary heart team meeting, including interventional cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, imaging specialists and anaesthesiologists.

Should the current prosthesis fail prematurely, treatment options would be extremely limited. Surgical explantation would remain technically demanding and high-risk. Emerging catheter-based solutions such as bioprosthetic valve fracture or leaflet laceration (eg, bioprosthetic or native aortic scallop intentional laceration to prevent iatrogenic coronary artery obstruction (BASILICA) might be considered, although their feasibility and safety in triple-stented configurations remain uncertain.
